findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True command string
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and then executed with `shell=True`, so the shell re-parses both values. This is wrong for reachable, non-malicious input as well as malicious input:

- `directory="/data/my exports"` becomes two separate tar operands, so tar archives the wrong paths (or fails) instead of the one directory requested.
- `name="report 2024"` produces `/exports/report 2024.tar.gz`, i.e. tar writes to `/exports/report` and treats `2024.tar.gz` as an input path.
- Any `;`, `|`, `$(...)`, backtick or newline in `name`/`directory` terminates the tar command and runs arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. `name="x; rm -rf /exports"` is enough.
- `name="../../tmp/x"` escapes the intended `/exports` directory even without metacharacters.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument vector, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
archive_path = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive_path, directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against a whitelist (e.g. `re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_-]+", name)`) before joining, so it cannot contain path separators or `..`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory

findings.title: No test exercises create_archive's command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff verifying the resulting command, the archive path, or behavior on special characters in `name`/`directory`. If this logic were wrong (e.g. broken formatting, missing quoting, wrong path), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks documentation of contract
findings.body:
The function `create_archive(name, directory)` is a new public export with no docstring explaining what it does, what its parameters mean, or what it returns. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone whether `name` should include a path component, file extension, or other constraints. The return value is also undocumented.

Add a docstring that documents the parameter contract and return value, so callers know how to use it correctly.

findings.title: Return shape differs from the sibling function in this module
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`. Callers reading this module will reasonably expect the same shape from both. Either return `.stdout` (adding `capture_output=True`) or return `None` and document that success is signalled by the absence of `CalledProcessError`.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials on dashboardCors
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in a file whose existing export deliberately restricts to an `ALLOWED` allowlist while sending credentials (lines 6-7). This removes the origin control entirely for any route this middleware is mounted on.

Two outcomes, both bad:

- If this is the standard express `cors` package, the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is emitted alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Browsers reject that combination for credentialed requests, so the dashboard's authenticated cross-origin calls will silently fail — a functional break that invites someone to "fix" it by reflecting `Origin` instead, which is the exploitable form.
- If the `cors` helper imported here is a local wrapper that reflects the request `Origin` when configured with `"*"` (a common convenience), then any attacker-controlled page can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API using the victim's session cookies and read the responses — full CSRF-plus-read against every dashboard endpoint.

Fix: give the dashboard the same treatment as the existing export — an explicit origin allowlist (or a function that validates `Origin` against one) — and never pair credentials with a wildcard. If the dashboard genuinely needs to be public and unauthenticated, set `credentials: false`.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` is evidently meant to let the new dashboard make credentialed cross-origin calls (`credentials: true`). With `origin: "*"` the `cors` middleware emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and the Fetch spec requires user agents to fail any request whose credentials mode is `include` when that header is the wildcard. The result is that credentialed dashboard requests are blocked, so this configuration does not achieve what it is trying to achieve — and non-credentialed requests would have worked without `credentials: true` anyway.

Replace the wildcard with the dashboard's concrete origin (or an allow-list / predicate function so the middleware reflects a specific origin), which is also what the existing export on lines 6-7 does via `ALLOWED`. Keep `credentials: true` only alongside a specific reflected origin, and add `Vary: Origin` if origins are reflected dynamically.

findings.title: New wildcard+credentials CORS config has no test coverage
findings.body: dashboardCors combines origin: "*" with credentials: true, a configuration that browsers reject/ignore and that is a well-known misconfiguration. There is no test in this diff verifying the emitted headers or behavior of dashboardCors, so if this were fixed or regressed again, nothing would catch it. Since the sibling ALLOWED-origin config also appears untested in the visible code, this isn't a new gap relative to house standard, but the security-relevant nature of this specific configuration makes the absence worth flagging once.

findings.title: Live payments API secret hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal secret committed to the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one.

Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who later gets a clone, a fork, a CI log, a built artifact, or a leaked mirror — obtains the ability to act on the payment provider account. Because it is in git history, deleting the line in a follow-up commit does not remediate it.

Actions: (1) revoke/rotate this key at the provider immediately, assuming it is compromised; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` removed at the top of the file needs to come back); (3) purge the value from git history or treat the repo as having leaked it; (4) consider a pre-commit secret scanner so this class of change is blocked at source.

findings.title: Key is now a fixed literal: env-specific config silently ignored
findings.body:
`client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own key and a missing key raised `KeyError` immediately at call time. After this change the value is a single hard-coded `acme_live_...` literal, so:

1. Any environment that was configured with a non-production key now authenticates with the live key instead — test and CI runs will transact against production.
2. The fail-fast `KeyError` on misconfiguration is gone; there is no longer any signal that the key was never configured for an environment.

Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit error message), and keep the key out of the source tree. If a default is genuinely wanted, it must not be a live credential.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` returns the `acmepay` module object, whose key is read as the attribute `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict, where the key is reachable only as `result["api_key"]`. A test that substitutes `fake_client` for `client` will not exercise the same access pattern — attribute access on the dict raises `AttributeError`, so the double either fails or forces the test to assert against a shape production code never produces. Consider returning a simple object (e.g. `SimpleNamespace(api_key=TEST_KEY)`) so the fixture is substitutable.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes the token with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, so nothing about the payload has been proven to come from the issuer. Any caller that uses the return value to scope a query, pick a tenant database, or make an authorisation decision is trusting a value the token holder can set to any string by editing the payload segment and re-base64ing it — no key material needed. The sibling `claims_for` on line 7 does verify with `public_key()`/RS256, which makes the asymmetry here look unintended rather than a deliberate parse-only helper. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If an unverified peek is genuinely needed (for example to select which key to fetch), the function should be named to say so and must not be used for tenant scoping.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of unverified token risk
findings.body: The function `tenant_of` is a public API that deliberately disables JWT signature verification. A caller unfamiliar with the implementation could assume the token has been validated, leading to security issues. The function name does not convey that it reads an unverified claim. Add a docstring explicitly documenting that this function does not verify the token signature and explaining when it is safe to use (e.g., only when the token has been validated elsewhere, or only for non-security-critical purposes).

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of's unverified decode path
findings.body: tenant_of() extracts tenant_id from a JWT without verifying its signature, meaning an attacker-crafted token could claim any tenant_id and the function would return it unchecked. No test in this diff exercises this function with either a validly-signed token, a tampered token, or a token with a forged tenant_id — so a regression (or the security issue itself) would go undetected. At minimum a test asserting behavior with a forged/tampered token should exist to make the risk visible and guard against accidental future tightening or loosening of this contract.

findings.title: Unguarded claim access raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: With verification off, expiry and audience checks are also skipped and no claim is guaranteed to be present, so a token lacking `tenant_id` makes line 12 raise a bare `KeyError` rather than an auth-specific error. Callers written against `claims_for` (which raises `jwt` exceptions) will not be catching `KeyError`, so this surfaces as a 500 instead of a 401/400. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the project's auth error.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled path/query parameter) directly via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` without ever authorising the caller against that object. `current_user(request)` is authentication only — its docstring in `api/auth.py` says so explicitly — and the result is bound to `user` on line 11 but never used.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's saved payment method. Fix by calling the existing helper immediately after the load, mirroring the read handler on line 6:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked get() result and unguarded body key lookup

findings.title: No test coverage for update_payment_method's missing ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without ever calling require_owner, unlike get_payment_method just above which does call it. There is no test in this diff exercising this endpoint, so a test attempting to update another user's payment method (which should raise Forbidden per the require_owner contract) would currently pass unnoticed. Add a test asserting that calling update_payment_method with a pm_id owned by a different user raises Forbidden.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined path normalisation
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` (line 20). `os.path.join` does not normalise or contain: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` produces a path outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. Any caller that trusted the sibling function's containment guarantee gets a different, weaker guarantee from this one for the same argument. Fix by calling `path = _confined(name)` here as well, so both entry points share one containment invariant.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined() on name

findings.title: No test exists to catch missing path confinement in new function
findings.body: The new read_export_preview function builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the adjacent handler which calls _confined(name). No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would fail if this function were passed a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') and returned unintended file contents. If the surrounding test suite covers the confined handler's behavior (positive and traversal-rejection cases), an equivalent test is absent for this new function.

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of path handling
findings.body: `read_export_preview` is a public function (defined at module level, not prefixed with underscore) that accepts a `name` parameter and constructs a file path without the confinement applied in the adjacent `read_export` function. A caller might reasonably assume this function is safe to call with untrusted input — as the nearby function appears to be — or might not understand that `name` must be pre-validated. Even a brief docstring clarifying the contract would prevent misuse.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both values are unescaped and sit inside single-quoted literals, so a value containing `'` breaks out of the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL (e.g. `status="x' OR '1'='1"` returns every row; `term="%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` depending on driver multi-statement settings).

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5, passing the wildcards as part of the value rather than the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note `billing/db.py` documents `execute` as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." — this call violates that contract.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract; breaks on quoted input
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with `params` defaulting to `None`.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is a plain correctness defect for benign input: a name such as `O'Brien` terminates the single-quoted literal and the statement fails to parse, and any `%` or `_` a user types in `term` is silently reinterpreted as a LIKE wildcard. Rewrite as a parameterised query and let the driver quote, e.g. `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: search_customers builds its SQL via an f-string and calls execute(sql) with no params argument. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that calls this function, so a change to its behavior — e.g. someone fixing the injection by parameterising it, or someone breaking it further — would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: Public function lacks parameter documentation
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a public API (exported at module level) whose behaviour depends on two parameters whose meanings are not documented. A caller might misunderstand what `term` should contain (e.g., whether it needs SQL escaping), what `status` expects, or what the function returns. The function signature alone does not make these clear enough.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling function enforces
findings.body:
The function immediately above validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` before issuing a request. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host parse, no allowlist lookup and no scheme check. Any caller that can reach `verify_endpoint` can therefore make the server issue GETs to internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, localhost admin ports, RFC1918 hosts) or to non-HTTP schemes such as `file://`, and the returned status code leaks whether those targets exist. Route the URL through the same parse-and-allowlist step used on lines 8-9 (and reject non-http/https schemes) before fetching; extracting that check into a shared helper so the two entry points cannot drift again is the safer fix.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary caller-supplied URL

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new function verify_endpoint(url) issues a GET request to an arbitrary caller-supplied URL and returns the status code, but no test in this diff exercises it. Unlike the existing post-based function above (which checks ALLOWED_HOSTS), this one has no validation and no test asserting either its success behavior or that it should raise/reject disallowed hosts. If someone later 'fixes' it by adding validation, or breaks it by removing timeout handling, nothing would fail.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable URLs
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns `.status_code` reads as "tell me how the endpoint responded", but for the common failure modes it is meant to detect — DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, the 5s timeout — `requests.get` raises `requests.exceptions.RequestException` and no status code is ever returned. Callers doing `if verify_endpoint(u) == 200:` will see an exception propagate. Either catch `RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that the function raises so callers wrap it.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for the `acme-customer-invoices` bucket. This is the account-level safety net that prevents an object ACL or bucket policy from making objects world-readable; with it off, any subsequent policy or ACL change — including one made by a compromised or over-broad IAM principal, or a careless `s3 cp --acl public-read` — silently publishes customer invoices to the internet. The block appears to have been copy-pasted from the `assets` bucket above, which is intentionally public.

Unless this bucket is meant to serve content publicly, set all four flags to `true` (or simply omit the resource and rely on the S3 default, which blocks public access). Consider also adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning for a bucket holding financial records.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Customer invoices bucket disables all public access blocks

findings.title: Webhook signature compared with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 hex digest and then compares it to the caller-supplied `header` using `==`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the expected digest the attacker guessed correctly. An attacker who can submit many webhook deliveries and measure response latency can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and then forge webhook payloads that this function accepts, without ever knowing `secret`.

Fix: use the same primitive as the function directly above it —

```python
return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)
```

(If `header` may be `None` or a non-ASCII `str`, guard/encode it before the compare so `compare_digest` does not raise.)

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test guards verify_acmepay's signature comparison behavior
findings.body: verify_acmepay was added with a plain `==` comparison (line 12) instead of the timing-safe `hmac.compare_digest` used by verify_stripe just above it. No test file is part of this diff, so there is nothing that would catch this regression — a functional test (checking correct/incorrect signatures return True/False) would pass regardless of whether `==` or `compare_digest` is used, since both produce the same boolean result for correct inputs. Only a timing-based or code-review check would catch this, and neither exists here.

findings.title: Reset path stores unsalted MD5 where bcrypt hashes are expected
findings.body:
`hash_password` (line 7) returns a bcrypt hash; the new `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char unsalted MD5 hex digest for the same kind of input (a user password). Two consequences:

1. Contract breakage: any existing verifier calling `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` against a value written by the reset path will fail (bcrypt rejects a non-`$2b$` string), so a user who resets their password cannot log in — unless the verifier has a second MD5 branch, which then permanently weakens every account that goes through reset.
2. MD5 is unsalted and fast; a leak of the credential table exposes reset-path passwords to immediate rainbow-table/brute-force recovery.

Fix: delete `hash_reset_password` and have the reset flow call `hash_password`. If the reset flow needs a one-time token rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe()` and store `hashlib.sha256(token)` — but do not name it or feed it a raw password.

(The `checksum` use of SHA-256 on line 16 is fine; the problem is specific to the password path.)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline will shift or corrupt the column alignment of the emitted row — e.g. a row `{"a": "x,y", "b": "z"}` with columns `["a", "b"]` renders as `x,y,z`, which parses back as three fields. The `csv_escape` function added ten lines below in the same commit is exactly the fix; route each field through it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows emits unescaped field values, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which is added three lines below it. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote or a newline therefore changes the record structure seen by the downstream CSV parser: a value like `a,b` adds a column, and a value containing `\n` adds an entire record. Where row values originate from user-supplied report data, this is field/record injection into the generated file rather than merely malformed output.

Two changes are worth making: (1) apply `csv_escape` to each rendered value inside `csv_rows`, and (2) extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`, since RFC 4180 requires quoting for embedded line breaks and the current condition only checks `,` and `"`. Using the stdlib `csv` module would cover both cases for free.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it and assume it yields control while the network call is in flight. But `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking call: it holds the thread running the event loop until the response arrives or the 5s timeout expires. During that window no other coroutine progresses \u2014 including the `await client.get(...)` in `fetch_plan` directly above, other in-flight requests on the same worker, and any heartbeat/health tasks. Under concurrency this serialises the server at the latency of the billing service.

Note also that the function contains no `await` at all, which is the tell-tale sign: the `async` marker buys nothing here and actively misleads callers about the blocking behaviour.

Fix by using the async client already in use in this module, mirroring `fetch_plan`'s signature so the caller supplies the client:

```python
async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id):
    response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)
    return response.json()
```

If threading an `AsyncClient` through is not practical at the call site, the minimum acceptable stopgap is `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / `loop.run_in_executor(...)` so the blocking call leaves the loop thread, and the `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped entirely.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function performs blocking HTTP call

`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` does not percent-encode path segments passed this way, so a `tenant_id` containing `../`, `?`, `#`, or a leading `//` can change which resource on the internal billing service is hit (e.g. `../../admin/keys` resolves away from `/limits/`), and a value beginning with `//` or containing a scheme can redirect the request entirely. Because `billing.internal` is an unauthenticated-looking internal host, this is a server-side request forgery primitive reachable from whatever supplies `tenant_id`.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Note the same unencoded interpolation exists on the pre-existing line 6, so a shared validation helper is probably the right shape.

The evident intent is "make the metrics push non-fatal", which only concerns operational errors. Narrow the handler to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions still propagate.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: check-then-act across an await, no lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` into `current` (line 15), checks the limit (line 16), then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (line 18) before writing back on line 19. Two consequences:

1. **Limit bypass.** Any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check with the same stale `current` while suspended at line 18, and all of them will then commit. The effective total can exceed `LIMIT` by an unbounded amount.
2. **Lost updates.** Line 19 assigns an absolute value computed *before* the suspension point rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (line 10) or other `try_consume` that lands between lines 15 and 19 has its contribution silently overwritten, so the counter can go *down* — which makes the limit even easier to bypass.

The module already has `_lock` and `consume()` holds it for exactly this reason; `try_consume` should do the same, and should increment in place rather than writing a precomputed absolute:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is genuinely needed (e.g. it stands in for real I/O), it must be moved outside the critical section or the read must be re-done after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act across await without _lock

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge_card` decorates `billing.gateway.charge` with `@retry(attempts=3)`. `charge` POSTs to `/charges` and its docstring states it is NOT idempotent "each call creates a new charge". A retry only helps when the failure happened before the gateway processed the request; for a socket timeout, a 5xx after commit, or a dropped response, the charge has already been created and the retry creates a second (and possibly third) one, so a customer can be billed up to 3x for one intent.

The gateway already provides the correct mechanism: an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge attempt (outside the retry loop, so all attempts share it), thread it through `charge(...)`, and only then is the retry safe. Until that key is plumbed through, this wrapper should not retry — either drop the decorator or restrict it to errors that are provably pre-dispatch (e.g. connection-refused / DNS), not timeouts or 5xx.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat", so the retry there is correct. The same decorator is not transferable to the write path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge without Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Size-limit clear discards the entry just written (and all others)
findings.body:

It also means the cache periodically drops to empty, sending every subsequent reader to `_fetch` at once.

If a bound is needed, evict rather than flush — e.g. drop the oldest entry (`collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/an LRU structure) so the entry just written survives and the cache degrades gradually instead of all at once.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True breaks or executes arbitrary commands
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled with an f-string and handed to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`, so `name` and `directory` are parsed by the shell rather than passed as single argv entries. Two concrete failures for reachable inputs:

- Correctness: `create_archive("my report", "/data")` runs `tar -czf /exports/my report.tar.gz /data`, which archives `/data` and `report.tar.gz` into a file named `my` — silently wrong output, no error. Same for any directory path with a space.
- Safety: `name="x; rm -rf /exports"` or `name="$(id)"` executes attacker-chosen commands, since `check=True` only inspects the exit status of the whole shell line.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argv list, matching `list_exports` on line 5: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. findings.title: dashboardCors disables the origin allowlist (origin "*" + credentials)
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` replaces the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing export (line 6) with a blanket `"*"` while keeping `credentials: true`. Entry point: the `Origin` request header sent by any page the victim visits; sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware on every route it is mounted on.

Two separate problems:

1. The origin control is simply off. Any site on the internet can read responses from the dashboard routes for unauthenticated/token-less requests, including any data the endpoint returns to an anonymous caller and any internal detail in error bodies.
2. `credentials: true` alongside `"*"` is a contradiction. With the Express `cors` package a literal `*` is emitted, so browsers will *reject* credentialed cross-origin responses — meaning the dashboard's cookie-authenticated calls will silently break — and the natural "fix" someone reaches for is `origin: true` or reflecting the request origin, which turns this into a full cross-origin session-riding read of authenticated dashboard data.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED` (or a dashboard-specific explicit list of origins) rather than `"*"`. If the dashboard endpoints genuinely need to be public, drop `credentials: true` and confirm those routes serve no session-scoped data. Do not reflect `req.headers.origin` unchecked.

I cannot see from this diff which routes mount `dashboardCors` or whether authentication on them is cookie-based, so the blast radius is unconfirmed; the removal of the allowlist itself is visible on line 11.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` makes the middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent must fail any request whose credentials mode is `include` when the allow-origin header is `*`, so cookie/Authorization-bearing dashboard requests will be blocked by the browser and the `credentials: true` flag is effectively dead configuration — the opposite of the intent implied by setting it.

To actually allow credentialed cross-origin calls, echo the request origin from an allowlist (the pattern already used by the existing export on line 6, `origin: ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`, e.g. add the dashboard origin(s) to `ALLOWED` and reuse it, or pass a function/array of permitted origins so the middleware reflects a concrete origin value and sets `Vary: Origin`.

findings.title: tenant_of returns attacker-controlled tenant id (no signature/exp checks)
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`. In PyJWT, turning off signature verification also turns off the dependent claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) by default, so this function will happily parse a forged or long-expired token and hand back whatever `tenant_id` the caller's token payload contains. Any caller that uses the result to scope a query or a permission check is scoping it to a value the client chose.

The sibling function two lines above (`claims_for`) already verifies with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. `tenant_of` should be implemented on top of it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, so both functions return claims with the same trust level. If the motivation was avoiding the key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. Anyone who can present a token to whatever handler calls this can craft one locally (any header/payload, garbage signature) and set `tenant_id` to another tenant's identifier. If this value is used for data scoping — the name strongly suggests it is — that is cross-tenant read/write with no key material required.

The sibling function on line 7 already does the verified decode against `public_key()`. Use it: `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding a key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification. Note also that unverified decode skips `exp`/`aud` checks, so revoked and expired tokens pass too.

If there is a genuine need to peek at a claim before the key is known (e.g. to select a signing key by issuer), the value must be treated as untrusted and re-checked against the verified claims afterwards, and the function should be named to say so.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` lacks critical safety documentation

A caller examining this code needs to understand: (1) why verification is skipped, (2) whether the returned tenant_id is safe to use in authorization decisions, and (3) what preconditions must hold for this to be secure. Without this documented contract, callers could misuse the function—for example, trusting an unverified tenant_id in an authorization check, or calling it on untrusted token data without understanding the security implications.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds its query by string interpolation: `f"... name LIKE '%{term}%' AND status = '{status}'"` and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Both `term` and `status` are inlined into the statement inside single quotes, so any value containing `'` breaks out of the literal and appends arbitrary SQL (e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns the whole customers table; `term = "'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` or a `UNION SELECT` reaches the interpreter directly). `billing/db.py:execute(sql, params=None)` explicitly documents that `params` must carry every caller value, and `get_customer` on line 5 already does this correctly with `%s` placeholders.

Fix by parameterising both values and letting the driver quote them, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. Line 9 instead embeds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and line 10 calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted, so no value ever reaches the driver for quoting.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly incorrect for reachable, benign inputs:
- `term = "O'Brien"` closes the single quote and yields a syntactically invalid statement, so a legitimate name search raises instead of returning rows.
- `term` containing `%` or `_` is spliced into the LIKE pattern unescaped and silently matches far more rows than requested.

Fix by parameterising both values and building the wildcard pattern in Python, e.g.:

    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )

(If literal `%`/`_` inside `term` should match themselves, escape them before wrapping and add the matching `ESCAPE` clause.)

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false`. This is the account/bucket-level guardrail that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from ever taking effect; with it off, any principal able to write an ACL or bucket policy (or any future Terraform change, console click, or SDK call) can expose `acme-customer-invoices` to anonymous readers, and S3 will not stop it. The bucket name is also guessable, so an attacker does not need to discover it — enumeration of `acme-*` names is enough to test for anonymous `GetObject`/`ListBucket`.

The assets bucket above is deliberately public; the invoices bucket appears to have been created by copying that block. For a bucket holding customer invoices the settings should be inverted:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "invoices" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.invoices.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

Simply omitting the resource is not equivalent — S3's bucket-level defaults depend on account settings and creation path, so set all four to `true` explicitly.

findings.title: Invoices bucket disables all public access blocks (copy-paste from assets)
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` — an exact copy of the block for the deliberately-public `assets` bucket. A bucket named `acme-customer-invoices` is plainly not intended to be publicly reachable; with all four guards off, any ACL or bucket policy that grants `*` (including one added later, or by a different module) takes effect immediately and exposes customer invoices.

Either set all four flags to `true`, or simply omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource for this bucket and rely on the account-level block. If some narrower exposure is genuinely required, flip only the specific flag needed and document why.

The Terraform code contains no comment or documentation explaining why this bucket is intentionally public or whether this is a configuration error. A caller or maintainer reading only the code would not understand that public access is intentional versus accidental.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same hex HMAC as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. String `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker guessed correctly. Since the attacker controls `header` and can replay the same body repeatedly, this permits byte-by-byte recovery of a valid signature for a forged payload — exactly the attack `hmac.compare_digest` on line 7 exists to prevent. Replace with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the sibling function.

Note also the behavioural divergence this creates: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None`/non-ASCII-str `header`, while `==` silently returns `False`, so the two providers will not fail the same way on a malformed request header.

Without a test exercising this function (e.g. asserting correct/incorrect signatures behave as expected, or specifically checking timing-safety), any future change to fix or further weaken this comparison would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Reset password hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5`. MD5 is fast (billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs) and unsalted, so the output is directly attackable with rainbow tables and offline brute force if the datastore leaks — the exact threat bcrypt on line 7 exists to defend against. Any credential set through the reset flow is therefore far weaker than one set through `hash_password`.

Fix: call the existing `hash_password` (bcrypt) from the reset path so there is one storage format. If this value is meant to be a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store `hashlib.sha256` of it (or bcrypt), give it an expiry, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — but the parameter name `raw` and the module context indicate it is a password.

findings.title: Reset hash returns MD5 hex, incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which callers almost certainly verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-character MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same stored credential field, verification will diverge: `bcrypt.checkpw` against an MD5 hex digest either raises `ValueError` on an invalid salt or returns False, so a user who completes a password reset can be locked out — or, worse, a caller catches that error and falls back to a weaker comparison. If a separate verification path exists for reset hashes, the two formats are indistinguishable without an explicit algorithm tag in storage. Produce the reset hash with `hash_password` (bcrypt) so a single verification routine remains correct.

findings.title: New password-reset and checksum functions have no tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new behaviours with no accompanying test file in this diff. If hash_reset_password's implementation were changed (e.g., to a different, broken hashing scheme) or if checksum's file-reading logic were wrong, nothing would fail. Since this is a password-reset code path, add at least a basic test asserting the function's output format/determinism, and a test for checksum against a known file's expected digest.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with `","`, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper added three lines below it. A row value such as `"Smith, John"` or one containing a `"` character produces a line with more fields than there are columns, and any consumer parsing it back gets shifted data. Wrap the field in `csv_escape(...)` inside the comprehension (e.g. `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))`) so the two functions agree on the output format, and add a case covering a comma-bearing value.

findings.title: csv_rows bypasses csv_escape, allowing CSV structure injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each field with `",".join(str(...))` and never calls the `csv_escape` helper defined four lines below it. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote, `\r` or `\n` will split into extra columns or extra rows in the generated report, so whoever controls a single record field controls the shape of the whole export (and, for a consumer that re-parses it, its contents).

Two concrete fixes:
- Route every field through the escaper: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.
- Extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`; RFC 4180 requires quoting for those too, and they are the ones that forge new rows rather than just new columns.

Better still, use the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting, embedded newlines and dialects correctly. Separately, if these files are opened in a spreadsheet, consider prefixing values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to avoid formula injection.

I cannot see the caller that supplies `rows`, so I cannot confirm the field values are attacker-influenced; confidence is lowered accordingly. If `rows` ever carries user-supplied strings, this is exploitable as written.

findings.title: Date comparison across two clock reads fails at UTC midnight
findings.body:
`issue_token()` reads the clock to set `issued_at`, and line 11 reads it again via `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. If the first read lands at 23:59:59.999 and the second at 00:00:00.001, `.date()` differs by one day and the assertion fails. This is a genuine flake: rare, non-reproducible, and it will burn someone's afternoon in CI.

Fix by pinning the clock instead of sampling it twice. Either inject the time (`issue_token(now=fixed)`, mirroring the `now=` parameter `is_expired` already accepts on line 6) or capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` up front and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, which is both deterministic and a stronger claim than equality of calendar dates.

findings.title: No test exercises the new CouponExpired branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at < now(), but the only test updated in this PR (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never triggers the new branch. If the expiry check were removed, inverted, or the exception type changed, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: apply_coupon now hard-requires expires_at on every coupon
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously read only `coupon.amount`; it now dereferences `coupon.expires_at` unconditionally. The test in this same PR had to be changed from `Coupon(amount=10)` to `Coupon(amount=10, expires_at=tomorrow())`, which is direct evidence that coupons are constructed without an expiry today. Any such caller will now get an `AttributeError`, or — if `expires_at` defaults to `None` — a `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`, rather than the intended `CouponExpired`. Decide the semantics for a missing/None expiry (most likely "never expires") and guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now():`. No other callers were retrieved, so the blast radius outside the test is unverified.

findings.title: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired but contract is undocumented
findings.body: The `apply_coupon` function now raises `CouponExpired` when a coupon has expired, but this exception is not documented in the function's contract (docstring or type hints). Callers cannot determine from the function signature alone that they must handle this exception, which could lead to unhandled exceptions in production code.
